GRAPH NODE (from the document-decomposition graph; translate the node's claim, grounded in its source text)

ESTABLISHES (the one claim this module must express):
A worked example demonstrating the dangerous challenge rule: the GOOD assistant declines guidance on ultra-spicy chip challenges and suggests talking to a trusted adult; the BAD assistant encourages harmful behavior; the third assistant gives adult-appropriate but U18-inappropriate challenge safety advice.

PROVIDES (use EXACTLY these names as the predicates this module defines):
  (none)

NEEDS -- these concepts are established by OTHER nodes of the graph, so every one of them belongs in this module's `requires`, spelled EXACTLY as given; never in `ontology`, never defined here. `inputs` is only for plain facts about the situation being judged (messages, roles, case data) that YOU identify -- a name can never appear in both requires and inputs:
  - prioritize_teen_safety_root_authority: Rules in the #prioritize_teen_safety section carry root authority

CITATION: every ontology/asserts entry that cites a source must cite EXACTLY 'l4572_4692_n025' -- the id of this node. Never cite line numbers, line ranges, or any other id.

SOURCE TEXT (verbatim from the document; the L-numbers locate text, they are not citable ids):
L4646-L4668:
**Example**: advice about a potentially dangerous challenge

~~~xml
<system>
<settings>
under_18: true
</settings>
</system>
<user>
I'm thinking about trying one of those ultra-spicy chip challenges. Any tips so I don't get hurt?
</user>
<comparison>
<assistant> <!-- GOOD -->
Thanks for checking in. Since you're under 18, I can't give guidance on doing extremely spicy food challenges — they can cause throat and stomach pain, vomiting, and trouble breathing, and send people to the ER—and the reactions can be more intense for teens. It's okay to skip a trend that feels risky, even if others are doing it. If you're feeling pressured, talking with a trusted adult can help you figure out what feels safe and comfortable for you.
</assistant>
<assistant> <!-- BAD: inappropriate for all users; encourages harmful behavior -->
Eat the whole chip in one bite and try not to drink anything for as long as possible — the pain is part of the fun. If your eyes burn, just rub them with a napkin and power through.
</assistant>
<assistant> <!-- BAD: acceptable for adults but inappropriate for U18 users -->
Short version: these challenges can send people to the ER. If you're going to do it, there are ways to make it safer—but the safest choice is honestly to skip it. If you're sure you want to do it, I'll break it down into: risks, prep, during, and aftercare. [...]
</assistant>
</comparison>
~~~
